# Abstract

In this paper we present an interactive framework for exploratory analysis of inferred transmission networks.

The reconstruction of person to person transmission is a widely studied subject and there are
a plethora of methods that infer and reconstruct outbreaks from various kinds of different data.

Our program provides a locally running web based interface that is easy to use,
provides interactive visualizations which can easily be extended with metadata information
and supports a wide variety of input formats.
Our software is user friendly, easily extendible and freely available online.

# Impact Statement

When reconstructing the transmission history of an outbreak it is important to easily investigate the inferred transmission pathways.
Having an easy to use and interactive dashboard to explore the results of an inference method
in combination with metadata about individuals can significantly improve the understanding of transmission pathways.
Our program, CONTAGION, is easy to use and run and makes the visualization of a who-infected-whom network
easy and available to a wide audience of users such as public health laboratories or medical researchers.

# Introduction

Understanding and reconstruction tranmission dynamics is an important component of infectious disease outbreak analysis.
A wide range of computational methods have therefore been developed to reconstruct transmission histories from epidemiological, genomic and contact-tracing data (TODO citations too all, maybe add, for a recent but already outdated overview see duault et al.).
These methods have been developed for and applied to outbreaks across a variety of infectious diseases (both human and animal borne) and differ substantially in their input data, underlying models, and assumptions about the tranmission process(citations maybe describe the different diseases applications here).

Although these appraoches differ in how transmission is inferred, most try to reconstruct who-infected-whom as a representation of the transmission history.
This provides a common object through which transmission histories can be inspected, despite the substantial methodological differences between inference approaches.
In practice, however, the visualization and explortion of these networks is often closely coupled to the software used for their inference.
Different tools use different output formats and visualization approaches, making it difficult to explore or compare inferred transmission histories across methods using a consistent workflow.

This lack of a common visualization layer presents challenges for both exploratory analysis and comparison of tranmission-infernce methods.
Researchers may need to use different tools or construct separate visualisations depending on the software used to generate a network.
Moreover, visalizations are often presented as static images, requiring descisions about which transmission events, annotations, and other network properties should be displayed before the figure is generated.
Exploring alternative representations from the same analysis output can consequently require rerunning a whole workflow from scratch and resutling in the need to compare and investigate several images.
This is particularly limiting when investigating large networks or when the inferred transmission history is associated with substantial uncertainty and additonal epidemiological metadata.

Interactive visualization provides an opportunity to address these limitations by separating the exploration of a transmisson network from the software used to infer it.
Rather than committing to a single static representation, users can interactively explore different aspects of the same inferred network and adapt its visualization to questions being investigated which in term might generate new questions to investigate.
A common visualization interface layer can furthermore provide a consistent way to explore outputs from different inference approaches, facilitating their comparison without requiring method-specific visualization workflows.
Another potential benefit of a detached layer for downstream visualization is the development of tool agnostic statistics that can be integrated and made available for collection of tools from their common output rather than having to provide them individually to each inference tool.

Here, we present CONTAGION, an interactive visualization application for exploring who-infected-whom networks produced by multiple tranmission-inference software tools.
CONTAGION provides a common visualization layer between tranmssion-inference methods and the subsequent exploration of their results up to the generation of publication ready figures.
Outputs from different software packages can be translated into a comon network representation and explored through a unified interface.

The application provides interactive control over network visualization, including filtering tranmission events, changing edge-support thresholds, modifying node and edge annotations and shapes, and rearranging the networks layout.
Additional individual-level metadata can be incorporated into the visualization and used to explore the network and the inferred dynamics.
By bringing these capabilities together in a single application, CONTAGION allows users to interactively investigate tranmission networks without having to construct separate visualizations for each inference method or paramter threshold setting.

At the time of writing, CONTAGION supports outputs from several tranmission-inference approaches, including Scotti, outbreaker2, TransPhylo, and BREATH, as well as custom network representations (TODO might have to add more, thinking about phybreak for example, also want to support general dot files).

# Theory and Implementation

## Who-infected-whom networks

To understand transmission dynamics, studies infer transmission trees and aim to reconstruct who-infected-whom relationships, providing information that can help characterize outbreaks and target control and preventative measures.
These reconstructions can be represented as a directed graph, where nodes correspond to individuals and edges represent tranmission events from an infector to the individual they infected.
Such networks can be used to investigate transmission routes, characterize heterogeneous infectiousness and likely superspreading events, and identify important transmission contexts such as households or facilties.
At the population level, the network may also reveal clusters and larger structures within an outbreak.

For their reconstruction, different combinations of epidemiological and genomic information, including sampling dates, contact-tracing information, geographical information, and pathogen sequence data, are used.
Existing inference methods differ in how these sources of information are incorporated and in the assumptions made about the transmission process.
A recent review article of such methods groups them into three families: sequential phylogenetic, simulatenous phylogenetic, and non-phylogenetic approaches (TODO cite duault).

Inference typically involves uncertainty and therefore results in a multitude of possible transmission histories rather than a single definitive reconstruction.
These possible histories can be summarized as a transmission network that captures the uncertainty in the inferred relationships.
For example, outbreaker2 uses MCMC to sample transmission chains, while TransPhylo and BREATH can account for unsampled individuals in the reconstructed transmission tree.
The resulting transmission relationships should therefore be interpreted in the context of this uncertainty associated with the inference method.

Visualizing the inferred transmission networks alongside additonal information allows a comparison between the inferred and known or independently established information.
This can be useful for assessing whether particular tranmission relationships are compatible with known contact patterns, sampling dates, locations, or toher outbreak information.
Individual samples are also commonly associated with metadata describing the individuals involved, such as age, sex, geographical location, household, or sampling date.
Such information provides additional context for interpreting the inferred transmission history and can reveal patterns that are not apparent from the network structure alone.

## Our proposed layer of visualization

While inference methods focus primarily on reconstructing complex tranmission networks, researchers must subsequently explore and iterpret the resulting networks.
This exploration is often performed using static visualizations or separate, method-specific workflows.

Static network visualization require many aspects of the network to be fixed in advance.
For example, an edge posterior-support threshold may determine which transmission relationships are displayed, while node colours, metadata attributes, and network layouts are fixed for a particular figure.
Exploring a different combination of settings such as different thresholds, comapring different metadata, or rearranging a densly connected network therefore requires generating a new image from the beginning.
These limitations become particularly relevant for large networks, where changing the layout, manually repositioning nodes, or changing edge threshold values may help reveal individual transmission relationships and larger network structures.

We present CONTAGION as an interactive visualization layer for tranmission-inference methods.
It provides a common interface through which users can explore the inferred network, its uncertainty, and associated metadata without constructing separate visualizations for each analysis.
Inference-specific output formats are converted into a common representation, allowing the same visualization and exploration functionality to be applied across different inference approaches.

## Implementation details

Our application is implemented in Python using the Dash framework [@parmer2025dash] for the web interface and
Cytoscape.js [@franz2016cytoscapejs], through the dash-cytoscape component, for interactive graph visualization.
The application runs locally or can be deployed as a web service, allowing users to explore the networks
directly within a browser.

Internally, the software has a modular architecture separating data handling, visualization, and user interface logic.
Each upload parser converts the inferred transmission data into a standard graph representation of nodes and edges.
Metadata is added to the node data and this representation is then shared between visualization and analytical components.
Interactive components such as filtering, coloring, metadata inspection, and network statistics
(e.g. node degree distributions or metadata-specific graph connectivity) are implemented through Dash callback functions that reactively update only the affected interface elements.

The application is open source (under a TODO license) and easily extendable to new input types, since each upload format has its own parser but all parsers use the same graph representation format.
All code and a tutorial website with associated data is available on github [https://github.com/Lars-B/interactive-wiw].
The application is also packaged, via a GitHub Actions build pipeline, into a single executable for each major platform, available for download from the repository releases [https://github.com/Lars-B/interactive-wiw/releases/latest].

# Discussion

<!-- Contribution and why tool is good idea -->
Inference methods for the reconstruction of infectious disease outbreaks are increasingly becoming more diverse with many available software tools TODOcite.
Interactive visualization approaches provide an important complement to these computational methods for analyzing the inferred transmission reconstruction together with additional metadata.
While statistical and phylogenetic approaches can infer the transmission relationships, visual exploration remains valuable for understanding the resulting structures and communicate findings.
Our application CONTAGION bridges this gap by providing an input agnostic interface to examine and explore inferred who-infected-whom networks interactively.
A common interface for these different methods in a valuable way to analyses and investigate findings for users but also an important tool when sharing findings with others in a unified way.

<!-- Where does it fit in and who is this for -->
Our tool, CONTAGION, separates the visulaization of a transmission network from the software tool used to infer the network.
This allows networks generated by different approaches to be inspected using the same visual conventions and interaction mechanisms,
making comparisons between results from different methods easier.
Rather than each method having to provide its own visualization, a shared visulaization framework provides a common interface for examining transmission scenarios.
A further advantage of CONTAGION is its accessibility to users without programming or terminal experience.
The browser-based interface allows transmission networks to be explored without writing code,
while the configurable interface allows users to adapt the visualization to different datasets and use cases.

<!-- strengths of our app approach -->
Existing transmission-reconstruction software may provide visualization functionality, while general-purpose network visualization tools can also be used to display transmission networks.
CONTAGION combines the strenght of both in focusing specifically on inferred who-infected-whom networks and in providing a common interface across multiple transmission reconstruction methods.
An additional advantage of a shared visualization framework is that it can make aspects of a reconstruction that are implicit in the underlying model more accessible to users.
In particular, CONTAGION provides a means of investigating indirect transmission relationships represented in the transmission trees produced by transphylo and BREATH.
These relationships might not be immediately apparent when examining the underlying output alone.
Using the same visualization framework also promotes consistency in how transmission reconstructions are presented,
reducing ambiguous or unclear differences in visual representation that arise solely from the different software used to generate it.

<!-- Limitations of our app -->
Our browser based architecture introduces a practical limitation.
Specifically for phylgenetic tree inference the output files are often large and require substantial time to upload and parse.
Browser based file handling may limit the size of datasets that can be conveniently explored.
These limitations represent a trade-off for the accessibility and ease of use provided by a browser-based application.
The need to support method-specific output formats also illustrates the potential value of standardized transmission-network representations.
Such a common representation could facilitate interoperability between inference methods, visalization tools, and downstream analysis.

<!--Future directions and wrap up -->
A natural extension of this application would be to include quantitavie summaries and comparison measures directly into the application.
For example, network-level statistics and metric used to compare transmission reconstructions could allow users not only to visually inspect networks,
but also to assess similarities and differences between reconstructions.
CONTAGION complements rather than competes with inference methods by providing a
common interface through which their outputs can be explored, interpreted, compared, and communicated.
